newsitem.title: FRANCE: Captains of industry clash in French merger talks.
newsitem.headline: Captains of industry clash in French merger talks.

text.p: Top French businessmen are battling in public over the terms of one of the country's biggest mergers marking a departure from France's tradition of private back room deals.
Jerome Monod, the discreet 66-year old chairman of water and construction group Lyonnaise des Eaux, hit back indirectly on Thursday at Saint-Gobain chairman Jean-Louis Beffa.

Monod is deeply involved in merger talks with Cie de Suez, a difficult and delicate operation which could crown his career at the utilities group with a deal that would push the group into the top 10 of French companies by market value.

Beffa, chairman of glass maker Saint-Gobain which has a 6.3 percent stake in Suez, on Tuesday called for a special dividend of some 3.4 billion francs ($603.7 million) to be paid by Suez to its shareholders before a merger.
Beffa claimed he also spoke on behalf of bank BNP and insurer Axa-UAP.

The comments were widely reported in newspapers and affected the share price of both Suez and Lyonnaise as analysts had been betting on a deal based on two Suez shares for one Lyonnaise and had seen Suez' cash as a key factor for merger's success.
Monod, adressing a news conference on the company's 1996 results, did not mention Beffa by name.
But his comment that any special payment would change the merger terms and a direct reference to the confidentiality clause to which board members are bound, left no doubt about his feelings.
Beffa sits on the Suez board. The 55-year old engineer is known for his outspoken opinions. He was among the three big Suez shareholders who brought down former chairman Gerard Worms in June 1995.

Beffa, UAP chairman Jacques Friedmann and Elf-Aquitaine head Philippe Jaffre publicly called on Worms to resign after the latter had failed to inform the Suez supervisory board of alliance talks with Francois Pinault.
He was also a member of the committee of five who selected and appointed Gerard Mestrallet as the current Suez chairman.
Mestrallet, tipped by some to become head of the merged group, knows that he cannot totally ignore the wishes of the shareholders who supported him.
The 48-year old Parisian, a former civil servant, had impressed the Suez shareholders with his running of Societe Generale de Belgique (SGB) since 1991.

While he lacks the political clout in France of a Monod, who is a close friend of president Jacques Chirac, Mestrallet is very well connected in Belgium and is using his contacts to placate Belgian polticial worries about the future of SGB and the country's main utility group Tractebel, controlled by Suez.
Beffa, meanwhile, is in a somewhat tenuous position on the Suez board. The biggest corporate shareholder in Saint-Gobain, with 8.3 percent, is Lyonnaise's bigger rival Generale des Eaux.

And Generale's chairman Jean-Marie Messier, while denying reports he actively sought to torpedo the Suez-Lyonnaise deal, has said in public he would only bring Generale's Suez shares to the deal if minorities were rewarded. ($ = 5.631 French Francs)
